doc.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Volume in fusion bands
summary: Ear-ringing volume with Cobham and a painful Al DiMeola and Jan Hammer concert made him play quieter.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Have you ever had any trouble with playing the fusion type thing and volume and all that?

Oh yeah. Yeah, I mean, well I used to play with Cobham and sometimes you’d come off a gig and your ears would be ringing. And the roadie would come over and say, “Congratulations, you’ve gone beyond the threshold of pain for the third concert in a row.” And I’d say no wonder. And now I play, yeah, not I just won’t play so loud. I mean there’s only so loud I’ll play because it hurts my ears. There are certain frequencies that hurt my ears. I guess high frequencies really just go right through them. I remember a concert with Al DiMeola and Jan Hammer that I went to in San Francisco and I don’t even think they were playing probably as loud on the stage as it was pumped out into the PA. And people were sitting there with their fingers in their ears listening to the concert. And some of them were just kind of like yeah man, grooving. And it was I was like I felt like someone had taken daggers and had jabbed them through my eyes, it was just like so painful I mean I just kind of I didn’t want to have anyone see me I was kind of like really got down real low and crept out of the theater, just went away and said I can’t listen to this. And maybe not at the fault of the musicians, you know it was just so loud. And I decided I never want to play music that loud, ever. It just has no place for me, I don’t get it. And I have played it that loud.
